title: Why Burnham should back Britain's new clean energy system, not more North Sea drilling
gist: New UK prime minister Andy Burnham faces cross-party and White House pressure to expand North Sea oil and gas drilling, but government data show the basin is 93% depleted with falling tax revenue and jobs, making a decentralized renewables-and-electrification build-out the larger economic opportunity.

themes.theme: The political fight over North Sea drilling

insights.claim: New UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham took office amid speculation over whether he would greenlight new North Sea oil and gas exploration licences, reform the windfall tax, or roll back Labour's 2024 manifesto pledge against new exploration licences, though the topic was notably absent from his first speech.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Watch for any reversal of the 2024 no-new-licences pledge as a signal of UK energy policy direction under the new premiership.

insights.claim: The Conservatives, led by Kemi Badenoch, have pledged to scrap the UK's 2050 net zero target and positioned themselves as champions of the oil and gas industry, framing their by-election win in Aberdeen South as a 'referendum on oil and gas'.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Signals oil and gas support is becoming a partisan wedge issue that could sway UK energy policy regardless of underlying resource economics.

insights.claim: Former Labour prime minister Tony Blair broke with the current Labour government's climate stance, calling for slower emissions reductions and for extracting 'what is left' of North Sea fossil fuels.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Shows the pro-drilling pressure on Burnham comes from within Labour's own ranks, not just political opponents, raising the odds of a policy compromise.

insights.claim: US President Donald Trump publicly pressured the UK on North Sea policy, posting on Truth Social amid rumours Burnham would approve new drilling that it was 'a big day for the country' and that people in Aberdeen were 'dancing in the streets'.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: US political pressure adds a geopolitical dimension to what is otherwise a domestic UK resource-economics decision.

insights.claim: Sources close to Burnham indicated no decision had been made and that he was expected to uphold Labour's manifesto pledge against issuing new North Sea exploration licences.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Base case appears to be policy continuity rather than a pivot toward expanded drilling, despite loud pressure from multiple directions.

themes.theme: The economic reality of a depleted North Sea

insights.claim: IEA executive director Dr Fatih Birol argued the UK debate is misplaced on the North Sea because remaining reserves offer no protection against high and volatile energy prices, stating publicly that 'Electrification not North Sea oil is future of UK energy'.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A leading global energy authority is explicitly discounting North Sea expansion as a price-stability or growth strategy for the UK.
insights.quote: Electrification not North Sea oil is future of UK energy - Dr Fatih Birol
insights.locator: At a recent Chatham House event

insights.claim: UK Continental Shelf oil and gas production peaked in 1999 and has been in gradual decline ever since, a trend driven by geology rather than net zero policy.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Frames North Sea decline as structurally geological, meaning policy reversals on licensing are unlikely to change the long-term production trajectory.

insights.claim: According to the UK government regulator, roughly 93 percent of the oil and gas the North Sea is likely to ever produce has already been extracted.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Quantifies just how limited the remaining upside is for any new drilling push, regardless of licensing policy.

insights.claim: The regulator estimates new North Sea drilling could yield around 74 million tonnes of oil and 381 TWh of gas in total, equivalent to only about half a year of UK consumption.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Puts a hard ceiling on the practical energy-security or economic benefit of new licensing rounds, undercutting the case for greenlighting new drilling.

insights.claim: Annual North Sea oil and gas revenues to the UK Exchequer are projected to fall to just £0.3 billion by 2030-31, down from £4.4 billion when Labour took office in 2024 and £9.1 billion when the Conservatives took office in 2010, and new licences will not materially change this trajectory.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: North Sea oil and gas is becoming fiscally immaterial to the Exchequer within five years regardless of licensing policy, weakening the revenue argument for expanded drilling.

insights.claim: North Sea sector employment fell by a third between 2014 and 2023 despite hundreds of new licences being issued in that period, and the diminishing economic gains now flow to a shrinking subset of companies and workers concentrated in a single UK region.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Historical evidence undercuts the jobs-protection argument for new licensing: past licensing rounds did not stop the employment decline.

themes.theme: The case for a decentralized renewable energy system

insights.claim: Renewable-energy-based power systems tend to be inherently less centralized than fossil-fuel-based systems, driven both by weather patterns and by the efficiency logic of siting generation and storage close to where it is needed.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A renewables build-out naturally aligns with Burnham's 'Manchesterism' agenda of decentralizing UK political and economic power, giving it political tailwinds beyond climate policy.

insights.claim: Solar generation is best sited in southern England while wind generation is concentrated in northern England, Scotland, and the North Sea, spreading renewable infrastructure and its associated economic activity geographically across the UK.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Geographic dispersion of renewable assets means the tax base and construction jobs are distributed nationally rather than concentrated in one region, unlike North Sea oil and gas.

insights.claim: Battery storage, an essential partner to variable renewable generation, tends to be built close to major demand centres like cities, which reduces electricity transmission losses and limits the need for costly new grid infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Storage-near-demand siting lowers system costs for consumers, an efficiency argument for continued battery storage investment.

insights.claim: Because renewables infrastructure is geographically dispersed, the tax revenue it generates, such as business rates paid to local authorities, is spread across the country rather than concentrated in one region.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Offers local authorities nationwide a fiscal incentive to support renewables build-out, broadening the political coalition behind the transition.

insights.claim: The flexible, modular nature of renewable energy technology supports a range of ownership models, allowing economic benefits to flow directly to citizens and communities rather than only to large energy companies.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Community and citizen ownership models in renewables could become a distinct investable structure distinct from traditional utility-scale ownership.

themes.theme: Jobs and the next phase of the energy transition

insights.claim: The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) estimates the UK's net zero economy directly supported around 308,000 jobs in 2025, with a further 520,000 jobs in the supply chain and 234,000 more in the wider economy, spanning renewable installation, maintenance, manufacturing, engineering, construction and professional services.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Quantifies a net zero jobs base already roughly 3.5x larger than what North Sea oil and gas has historically supported, positioning green jobs as the larger UK employment story.

insights.claim: The UK has made strong progress deploying renewable generation on the supply side, but much less progress electrifying heating and transport on the demand side, implying many more transition-related jobs are still to be created in this next phase.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Demand-side electrification (heat pumps, EV infrastructure) is the underbuilt segment of the UK energy transition and a likely area of future policy focus and investment.
